title: Overview
heading: Overview
body: quarry is a desktop IDE for Rust and C/C++ only, built to match CLion on the loop you run every day: open a project, navigate it, read the errors, fix them, build, run a test, start the debugger, look at memory. It is not a general editor, and it does not try to match CLion's feature count. The three things a CLion user would miss after moving — clangd-grade C/C++ insight, rust-analyzer-grade Rust insight, and an LLDB debugger with variables, watchpoints, disassembly and a hex memory view — are exactly what it is built around. Those engines already exist; quarry is the IDE around them. quarry probes PATH and then xcrun for rust-analyzer, clangd, lldb-dap, rustfmt, clang-format, cargo, cmake and ninja. Nothing is vendored, so the versions you debug with are the versions your project builds

title: Overview
heading: What works today
body: Projects — open a folder, detect Cargo.toml, CMakeLists.txt or compilecommands.json, browse a lazily expanded tree, restore the last project, tabs and layout on launch. Editing — CodeMirror 6 with Rust and C/C++ highlighting, a breakpoint gutter, diagnostics as squiggles and gutter markers, format on save, rename, code actions, signature help, inlay hints, occurrence highlighting and multi-cursor. Insight — rust-analyzer and clangd, one session per server kind per project root, with hover, completion, go to definition, references, document highlights, symbols, type hierarchy and calls. Build and run — cargo build --message-format=json, CMake, or plain clang; Debug and Release profiles; run configurations with program, args, cwd and environment. Debugging — raw DAP against lldb-dap: breakpo

title: Overview
heading: What it deliberately leaves out
body: Remote development, embedded targets, CPU and memory profilers, databases, Docker, AI assistance, plugin APIs and every language other than Rust and C/C++. Naming them here is the point: a focused IDE is defined as much by what it refuses as by what it adds.

heading: What gets detected
body: Both language servers can run at once: a repository with a Rust crate and a C++ test harness in the same tree gets rust-analyzer for the crate and clangd for the C++ file, each rooted where its own signal was found.

title: Projects
heading: What gets detected
body: Signals are looked for to a bounded depth, skipping target, nodemodules, .git, build and out, so a monorepo root still finds the crates inside it without walking the whole tree.

title: Projects
heading: Language-server sessions
body: A session is keyed by server kind and root: rust::/path/to/project and clang::/path/to/project. Every request names its session, and a file is only offered to a server that serves its extension — rust-analyzer never sees Cargo.toml, clangd never sees a .rs file. That gate is what makes the status chip honest about what is actually running.

title: Projects
heading: Per-project settings
body: A project can carry its own overrides in .quarry/settings.json at its root. The file is optional; whatever it omits falls back to the global settings. It is the right place for a root that needs a different font size or dock layout from the rest of your projects.

title: Projects
heading: Per-project settings
body: quarry writes nothing else into a project directory. There is no index, no cache and no build database of its own; the toolchains keep their own.

title: Language servers
heading: Language servers
body: quarry speaks LSP directly over a framed pipe. There is no plugin layer: a server is started for a project root, given the files it serves, and asked the questions the editor needs. A session is keyed kind::root and started only when the root carries that kind's signal: rust-analyzer for a Cargo.toml, clangd for a compilecommands.json, CMakeLists.txt or a C/C++ source. Both can be running at once. Servers only ever receive files they serve. rust-analyzer gets .rs; clangd gets .c, .h, .cc, .cpp, .cxx, .hh, .hpp. An unserved path is never opened, changed or closed against a server, which is what keeps a .cpp file in a Rust-only project from being reported as a clangd error. heading: Known limits
body: Sync is full-document. Incremental sync is not implemented; it is worth doing only when a stall is measured, not in advance. evaluate is still broken for Rust through lldb-dap, which is why watch expressions are pinned variables rather than arbitrary expressions. See Debugging.

title: Debugging
heading: Debugging
body: quarry speaks raw DAP to lldb-dap, the adapter Xcode ships. One client drives Rust and C/C++, because both are LLDB targets underneath. Debugging launches the binary the build just produced, with the arguments and working directory from the selected run configuration. The launch is made against the real path of the project directory; /var/… and /private/var/… are different strings to lldb, and a mismatch leaves every breakpoint unverified. Line breakpoints — click the gutter. Set them before a session starts; they are applied when the adapter launches. Conditional and log breakpoints — a condition is evaluated by lldb, a log message prints without stopping. Data breakpoints (watchpoints) — watch a variable's address and stop when it is written. title: Debugging
heading: Breakpoints
body: Line breakpoints — click the gutter. Set them before a session starts; they are applied when the adapter launches. Conditional and log breakpoints — a condition is evaluated by lldb, a log message prints without stopping. Data breakpoints (watchpoints) — watch a variable's address and stop when it is written. LLDB reports the store's line, which is often the line after the assignment you had in mind.

title: Debugging
heading: Breakpoints
body: evaluate is broken for Rust through this adapter — it falls back to Objective-C++ and errors. Watch entries are therefore pinned variables, re-read on every stop, plus memory views. Arbitrary expressions are not available until a different adapter is measured.

title: Debugging
heading: Frames, scopes and stepping
body: The debugger imports LLDB's Rust formatter script at session start, so Vec, String and friends arrive as values rather than as raw structs. Without it they silently print as internals.

title: Debugging
heading: Memory
body: The memory view reads the target by address, paged, and renders a hex band with an ASCII column. Unmapped regions are drawn as such rather than as zeroes. It is available while the target is stopped, and it works regardless of whether the adapter advertises memory references.

title: Architecture
heading: Frontend layout
body: The editor is CodeMirror 6, loaded lazily so its language packages stay out of the first bundle. Panels that are not on screen — the debugger, the terminal, search, quick open, the palette — are lazy as well.

title: Architecture
heading: Protocols
body: Language servers are started by the backend, keyed by kind and root. Every request names its session, and a file is only sent to a server that serves its extension.

heading: Where the seams are

title: Architecture
heading: Where the seams are
body: Formatter dispatch is per language. JSON is formatted in the frontend; TOML needs taplo; Rust and C/C++ keep their toolchain formatters. Nothing falls back silently. Diagnostics have three sources — rust-analyzer, clangd, and cargo's JSON output — merged into one model, so Problems does not care which produced a message. Themes fill one token set. A token the theme omits keeps the default, and the first paint uses a hard-coded fallback rather than the settings file.

title: Architecture
heading: Testing
body: The Rust side has cargo test and clippy. The frontend has bun test over the pure helpers: ranking, argument splitting, hex, buffers, blame, search, test filters. Anything that needs a real language server or debugger lives in scripts/-smoke.ts, which only run by hand.

title: Contributing
heading: Contributing
body: quarry is a personal project with a narrow scope: an IDE for Rust and C/C++ that matches CLion on the daily loop. Changes that widen the scope — another language, a plugin API, remote development — are out of scope by design, not by accident. Nine steps, all of them required: file size, types, formatting, lint, frontend tests, and the four Rust steps (cargo fmt --check, cargo check --all-targets, cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings). One invocation reports the whole picture; a failing step prints its own tail. title: Contributing
heading: House rules
body: No file over 200 lines. scripts/check-file-size.ts fails on a new offender and on a stale exception in docs/refactor/oversized.txt, so the list only shrinks. Split Rust by module directories and stylesheets with bun scripts/split-css.ts. src/ only, with @/ mapped to ./src/. Logic in src/lib, rendering in src/ui, and the feature name kept on both sides. Bun only. No npm, and bun run only where the name collides with a builtin. A formatter is never a gate. bun fmt writes; bun fmt --check verifies. Never a measured number in a commit message. Name the gates, not their totals.

body: Installed apps trust the public key baked into the build. Rotating it orphans every installed copy, so the key is generated once and never regenerated.
